extracted.intended_audience: theologians, Christian apologists, and readers/students of scriptural interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative criteria Pascal uses for judging the authenticity, meaning, and typological interpretation of Scripture (esp. Old Testament → New). Intended for readers practicing theological hermeneutics and apologetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneity as evidence of authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of the world beginning to be distant, God provided a single contemporary historian, and appointed a whole people as guardians of this book, in order that this history might be the most authentic in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues that a book contemporaneous with the events and preserved by a single people is the most authentic history; contrasted with later fabulous historians (e.g., Homer) whose romances become uncertain over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity of patriarchs preserves historical memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The longevity of the patriarchs, instead of causing the loss of past history, conduced, on the contrary, to its preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because long lives meant children lived long with parents and conversed about ancestors, oral transmission was more reliable; fewer intervening generations reduce distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous writers vs. later compilers
rubrics_metrics.description: Every history which is not contemporaneous ... are false, and found to be false in the course of time. It is not so with contemporaneous writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal uses contemporaneity as a criterion for truth: books composed by witnesses or contemporaries are more trustworthy than later traditions or legendary compilations (e.g., Sibyls, Trismegistus).

rubrics_metrics.name: A book that 'creates a nation' testifies to antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between a book which an individual writes, and publishes to a nation, and a book which itself creates a nation. We cannot doubt that the book is as old as the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a text has served to form or identify a people, its antiquity and centrality to that people are evidence of its early origin and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity/transparency as marker of reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Josephus hides the shame of his nation. Moses does not hide his own shame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willingness to record one's own faults or national shame (e.g., Moses' unflattering accounts) is evidence of sincerity and therefore reliability; concealment suggests bias or apologetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of unfavorable content indicates genuine custodianship
rubrics_metrics.description: They preserve lovingly and carefully the book in which Moses declares that they have been all their life ungrateful to God... and that he has called heaven and earth to witness against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Jews' careful preservation of texts that condemn them is cited as proof of their fidelity to the text and not merely patriotic or self-glorifying censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual custody and chain (Masorah/Talmud) as authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masorah... the Talmud includes together the Mischna and the Gemara. A.D. 440... the universal consent of all the Jews, who are necessarily obliged to observe all that is contained therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A documented chain of transmission and communal acceptance (Masorah, Talmudic machinery) functions as evidence for the preservation and authority of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fulfillment and continuity as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The sceptre was not interrupted by the captivity in Babylon, because the return was promised and foretold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency of prophetic statements with historical sequence (e.g., captivity followed by promised return) is used to evaluate prophetic truth and its relationship to messianic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent lines of proof for typology
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the two [Testaments] at one stroke, we need only see if the prophecies in one are fulfilled in the other. ... That the Scripture has two meanings ... is shown by the following proofs: 1. Proof by Scripture itself. 2. Proof by the Rabbis. 3. Proof by the Kabbala. 4. Proof by the mystical interpretation which the Rabbis themselves give to Scripture. 5. Proof by the principles of the Rabbis... [6. Proof by the key which Jesus Christ and the Apostles give us.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal insists on corroboration from several sources — internal scriptural evidence, rabbinic testimony, mystical traditions, rabbinic principles, and the interpretive key offered by Christ/apostles — rather than relying on a single proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural 'two meanings' (literal and spiritual/typical)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Scripture has two meanings, which Jesus Christ and the Apostles have given, is shown by the following proofs...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal asserts that many Old Testament passages are both literal/temporal and spiritual/typical; recognizing both layers is central to Christian typological interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types: visible events as images of invisible realities
rubrics_metrics.description: God, wishing to show that He could form a people holy with an invisible holiness, and fill them with an eternal glory, made visible things. As nature is an image of grace, He has done in the bounties of nature what He would do in those of grace...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and natural events (e.g., Red Sea, deluge) function as 'types'—visible signs that prefigure spiritual realities and the coming redemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interpretive extremes: literalism and over-spiritualizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two errors: 1. To take everything literally. 2. To take everything spiritually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hermeneutic balance is required: neither crude literalism nor blanket allegorizing is acceptable; each passage must be judged on evidence and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstrative types to remote or forced analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some types clear and demonstrative, but others which seem somewhat far-fetched, and which convince only those who are already persuaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to types that are clear and demonstrative; be skeptical of far-fetched or ad hoc typologies (e.g., apocalyptic stretchings) that convince only predisposed readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not found doctrines on ambiguous or extravagant readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagances of the Apocalyptics, Preadamites, Millenarians, etc. -- He who would base extravagant opinions on Scripture, will, for example, base them on this...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid building sweeping doctrinal positions on isolated, ambiguous, or obviously strained scriptural passages; restraint is a criterion of sound exegesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prophets' own statements of obscurity as evidence of figurative meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that the Old Testament is only figurative... First, that this would be unworthy of God. Secondly, that their discourses express very clearly the promise of temporal blessings, and that they say nevertheless that their meaning will not be understood...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prophets explicitly state their meaning is obscure or will be understood only 'in the fullness of time,' this indicates an intended typological/hidden sense beyond the plain historical reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions as signals to seek a higher (typical) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The third proof is that their discourses are contradictory, and neutralise each other; so that if we think that they did not mean by the words 'law' and 'sacrifice' anything else than that of Moses, there is a plain and gross contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When literal readings produce contradictions across passages, that conflict suggests the literal sense is not the ultimate sense, prompting a typological or reconciliatory interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile contrary passages as test of correct interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand the meaning of an author, we must make all the contrary passages agree... We must then seek for a meaning which reconciles all discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid interpretive solution should harmonize apparent contradictions; if no reconciliation exists under the literal sense, a different (typical/spiritual) meaning is indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermeneutic telos: the ultimate aim of Scripture is charity
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole aim of the Scripture is charity. All which tends not to the sole end is the type of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ethical/theological end (charity/love of God) as a guiding criterion: passages that do not directly tend to charity are likely typological shadows pointing toward that end.

rubrics_metrics.name: When literal statements are impossible/false, read them spiritually
rubrics_metrics.description: When the word of God, which is really true, is false literally, it is true spiritually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a literal reading leads to impossibility or falsehood (e.g., anthropomorphic locutions about God), prefer a spiritual interpretation that preserves theological truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic/Christ-given 'key' is final hermeneutic authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by the key which Jesus Christ and the Apostles give us... Jesus Christ opened their mind to understand the Scriptures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interpretive key supplied by Christ and the Apostles (their readings and teachings) is the decisive guide for reading Old Testament typology; apostolic interpretation legitimates certain spiritual senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual readiness/humility required to perceive types ('the veil')
rubrics_metrics.description: The veil, which is upon these books for the Jews, is there also for evil Christians, and for all who do not hate themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the hidden/typical sense requires self-knowledge, humility, and disposition (hating oneself); arrogance or self-satisfaction obstructs true understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees and features of types: portrait/ cipher notions
rubrics_metrics.description: A type conveys absence and presence, pleasure and pain. A cipher has a double meaning, one clear, and one in which it is said that the meaning is hidden... A portrait conveys absence and presence, pleasure and pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize structural features of types: they simultaneously signify presence and absence, have layered meanings (cipher), and may mix consolations and judgments; these rhetorical features help identify typological passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Letter kills, spirit gives life' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter kills. All happened in types. ... Not the meat which perishes, but that which does not perish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between external/literal observance (the 'letter') and the spiritual reality intended; the spiritual (that which 'does not perish') is the true object of divine law and prophecy.
